oneLineAnswer: An amino acid the body turns into serotonin, sold as a supplement; evidence for its effects is limited.
whatItDoes: Your body makes 5-HTP from tryptophan, an amino acid you get from food.
Enzymes convert 5-HTP into serotonin, and vitamin B6 is needed for that step.
Taken as a supplement, 5-HTP reaches the brain and raises serotonin production there.
Supplement 5-HTP is usually extracted from the seeds of Griffonia simplicifolia, an African plant.
NCCIH describes 5-HTP supplements as having sedative effects, but says how they work is unclear.
whatWeDoNotKnow: NCCIH says there is very limited data on 5-HTP's effects on insomnia, and that how it works is unclear.
PubChem's summary calls the antidepressant mechanism a hypothesis, not an established finding.

I read registry listings, not published outcomes, so this page cannot say whether any trial found a benefit for anyone. The studies I found were small: 33 healthy volunteers in one, 175 people with inflammatory bowel disease in another.
No source I fetched reported long-term safety data for 5-HTP.

No source I fetched gave 5-HTP-specific information about combining it with medicines that raise serotonin. NCCIH does warn that L-tryptophan supplements may cause life-threatening serotonin toxicity with medicines that affect serotonin metabolism, and that warning names L-tryptophan, not 5-HTP.

Nothing I fetched shows 5-HTP is an FDA-approved medicine. The only 5-HTP products in the FDA label database are homeopathic over-the-counter remedies, and their own labels say their claims are not FDA evaluated.

evidence.claim: 5-HTP is a tryptophan derivative carrying a hydroxy group at position 5, and has a role as a neurotransmitter and a human metabolite.
evidence.quote: 5-hydroxytryptophan is a tryptophan derivative that is tryptophan substituted by a hydroxy group at position 5.

evidence.claim: The body produces 5-HTP from the essential amino acid L-tryptophan, and 5-HTP is the immediate precursor of serotonin.
evidence.quote: 5-Hydroxy-L-tryptophan is an aromatic amino acid naturally produced by the body from the essential amino acid l-tryptophan.

evidence.claim: An enzyme called aromatic-L-amino-acid decarboxylase converts 5-HTP to serotonin, and vitamin B6 is required for that conversion.
evidence.quote: by the enzyme aromatic-L-amino-acid decarboxylase with the help of vitamin B6

evidence.claim: 5-HTP passes the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin inside brain cells.
evidence.quote: 5-HTP readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, and is converted to serotonin in brain cells.

evidence.claim: The therapeutic form of 5-HTP used in products is isolated from the seeds of the African plant Griffonia simplicifolia.
evidence.quote: The exogenous therapeutic form is isolated from the seeds of the African plant Griffonia simplicifolia.

evidence.claim: PubChem summarises 5-HTP as an aromatic amino acid with antidepressant activity, acting by conversion to serotonin or by binding serotonin receptors in the central nervous system.
evidence.quote: Oxitriptan is an aromatic amino acid with antidepressant activity.

evidence.claim: A PubChem summary reports that absorption of 5-HTP is roughly 47 percent to 84 percent, and that absorption happens by an active transport process.
evidence.quote: The efficiency of absorption of 5HTP, as well as its decarboxylation product serotonin, is approximately 47% to 84%.

evidence.claim: PubChem records the molecular formula of 5-hydroxytryptophan as C11H12N2O3 with a molecular weight of 220.22.
NCCIH states that 5-HTP supplements have sedative effects, that how they work is unclear, and that there is very limited data on their effects on insomnia.
evidence.quote: have sedative effects, but it is unclear how they work and there is very limited data on their effects on insomnia

evidence.claim: NCCIH has kept watch on 5-HTP for safety because of its chemical and biochemical relationship to L-tryptophan.
evidence.quote: Because of its chemical and biochemical relationship to L-tryptophan, 5-HTP has been under close watch for its safety.

evidence.claim: NCCIH reports that extensive analyses of several sources of 5-HTP found no toxic contaminants similar to those associated with L-tryptophan, and no other significant impurities.
evidence.quote: Extensive analyses of several sources of 5-HTP have shown no toxic contaminants similar to those associated with L-tryptophan

evidence.claim: NCCIH states that L-tryptophan supplement use stopped in 1989 after an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome traced to contaminated synthetic L-tryptophan from a single manufacturer.
evidence.quote: The use of L-tryptophan as a dietary supplement was discontinued in 1989 because of an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS)

evidence.claim: NCCIH classes L-tryptophan supplements as a serious safety concern, saying they may cause life-threatening serotonin toxicity when used with medicines that affect serotonin metabolism. The warning names L-tryptophan, not 5-HTP.
evidence.quote: L-tryptophan supplements (which may cause life-threatening serotonin toxicity when used with medicines that affect serotonin metabolism)

evidence.claim: The FDA drug label database contains four label records that list oxitriptan, the international nonproprietary name for 5-HTP, and all four are human over-the-counter products rather than approved prescription medicines.
A homeopathic 5-HTP product listed in the FDA label database states that its claims rest on traditional homeopathic practice, are not accepted medical evidence, and are not FDA evaluated.
evidence.quote: Claims based on traditional homeopathic practice, not accepted medical evidence. Not FDA evaluated.

evidence.claim: ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed Phase 2 trial testing oral 5-HTP against placebo in 175 people with inflammatory bowel disease in clinical and biological remission, with fatigue score as the outcome. The record does not report trial results.
evidence.quote: placebo cross-over trial aims to study the effect of the oral intake of an essential amino-acid 5-OH tryptophan

evidence.claim: ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed study of sub-chronic effects of 5-hydroxytryptophan on mood and emotional processing, enrolling 33 healthy volunteers.
evidence.quote: Sub-chronic Effects of 5-hydroxytryptophan on Mood and Emotional Processing in Healthy Volunteers

evidence.claim: DailyMed, the NLM label repository, indexes two products whose names contain 5-hydroxytryptophan, both homeopathic liquid preparations.

confidenceBasis: The main claims are each supported by two or more independent fetched sources: PubChem (two CID records), NCCIH, openFDA/DailyMed, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Confidence here covers factual grounding, not strength of evidence for any health effect, which the sources themselves describe as limited.
gaps: No dedicated NCCIH 5-HTP fact sheet exists at https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/5-htp or https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/highlights/5-htp; both returned HTTP 404. 5-HTP appears only inside NCCIH's sleep disorders material.
The Internet Archive Wayback index returned HTTP 503 (service offline), so older archived versions of any retired NCCIH 5-HTP page could not be inspected.
The DailyMed SPL detail endpoint returned HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type for the Energique record, so that specific label was verified through the openFDA mirror of the same label instead.

No MedlinePlus health topic or medical test summary mentioning 5-HTP was found. The MedlinePlus health topic search service returned zero results for the term 5-HTP. MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded from this work by instruction.
The ClinicalTrials.gov records fetched do not report outcome data, so no claim is made here that 5-HTP did or did not help participants in any study.
No source I fetched addressed pregnancy, breastfeeding or children beyond a generic homeopathic-label warning, and none addressed 5-HTP-specific interactions with serotonergic medicines.
I could not ground any claim about the quality, purity or actual 5-HTP content of currently sold 5-HTP supplement products.
I could not ground a claim that 5-HTP is an approved medicine anywhere; the only regulatory records found are human over-the-counter homeopathic products.
The 1989 eosinophilia-myalgia event is documented by NCCIH only in relation to L-tryptophan, not 5-HTP, and that distinction is preserved in the text above.
Nothing on this page is individualised dosing, diagnosis or treatment advice, so no such section was written and none is available from these sources.
